rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.4 and 3.1 <U+2014> the authors build their own GMS/MODFLOW model of the Qalyubia aquifer, calibrate it in steady state against 11 observation wells (Fig. 7) and verify it against 5 wells (Fig. 8), then run scenarios for 8 districts (Table 3, Fig. 10).
rows.notes: The study does not measure or otherwise observe recharge under drip versus flood irrigation. The lower recharge under modern irrigation is a model input assumption (Section 3.2: recharge in a district switched to modern irrigation is set to zero because it is 'almost zero', and pumping reduced 40% based on ref [16]); the flood-irrigation recharge of 0.1 mm/day is likewise taken from literature [15] and adjusted. The study's own result is the simulated head decline (10-50 cm) that follows from that assumption, and this scenario output is never compared with measurements from fields actually under drip/modern irrigation; only the base (flood) case is calibrated against observed heads. Hence the claimed recharge difference is presupposed rather than demonstrated, so Q2 is 'no'. Also note the study models 'modern irrigation' generically rather than drip specifically, although drip is named as one of the modern methods. The authors do state a condition from their results (clay-cap depth governs the magnitude of the effect, Conclusions) and a limitation (future domestic/industrial demand not considered, Discussion), but these are not credited because Q2 is 'no'. No dispersion measures reported.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a calibrated regional groundwater model (Qalyubia Governorate, Nile Delta) whose modern-irrigation scenarios impose zero recharge as an input; the recharge contrast between flood and drip is assumed, not an empirical finding of the study.
